name: National Mineral Resources Development Policy 2022 - value addition pillar
description: Objective 7 of the 2022 policy is to 'promote value addition in the mineral resource value chain', framing downstream processing, local content and eventually EV-battery manufacturing as core goals alongside the 3-million-tonne copper target. Analysts note implementation ambiguity over which ministry owns the value-addition agenda, and that almost no Zambian firms add value beyond copper cathode.
entities: Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development
source_name: Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development - National Mineral Resources Development Policy 2022 (PDF)
note: Primary source (official policy PDF). Critical academic assessment: Clube (2024), 'Value addition for who?', Extractive Industries and Society, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2214790X24001503

name: 10% export duty on copper ores and concentrates (Customs and Excise Act)
status: in force (suspended by waiver since August 2025)
description: Zambia levies a 10% export duty on copper concentrates under the Customs and Excise Act, explicitly designed as an industrial-policy lever to make raw concentrate export unattractive relative to domestic smelting. The duty's bite depends on domestic smelter capacity; when smelters are down, government has waived it rather than let concentrate stockpile.
entities: Ministry of Finance and National Planning
source_name: Mining.com / Reuters - Zambia extends duty-free copper concentrate export duty waiver
note: Snippet-based. Rate confirmed at 10% (not 15%) in 2025-2026 trade press; original introduction year of the concentrate export duty not pinned down in sources reviewed. The duty's beneficiation logic applies mainly to sulphide ores (concentrated then smelted); oxide ores are typically leached to cathode via SX-EW on site and never pass through the concentrate stage, so the lever bites unevenly across ore types.

name: Copper concentrate export duty waiver 2025-2026 (smelter outages)
description: First implemented in August 2025 and extended to 30 September 2026, the waiver suspends the 10% export duty for an approved quota of 271,742 tonnes of copper concentrates so miners can clear stockpiles while major smelters (including Kansanshi and Mopani units) undergo extended maintenance. Commentators read it as prioritising output and cashflow over beneficiation.
entities: Ministry of Finance and National Planning
source_name: bne IntelliNews - Zambia extends copper concentrate export-duty waiver
note: Snippet-based; corroborated by Mining.com and CNBC Africa. Evidence of the tension between the export-duty beneficiation lever and real smelting capacity.

name: 5% import duty on copper and cobalt concentrates (2019)
description: The 2019 budget imposed a 5% import duty on copper and cobalt concentrates from 1 January 2019, intended to capture more value from imported DRC feedstock. It backfired for value addition: ERG's Chambishi Metals refinery (capacity 6,800 t/y cobalt, 55,000 t/y copper), which processed DRC concentrate, suspended operations and placed 351 workers on paid leave; the Chamber of Mines warned of over 21,000 job losses from the wider 2019 tax package.
source_name: Fastmarkets - ERG suspends copper, cobalt production at Chambishi
note: Snippet-based. Key case study of a duty intended to promote domestic value capture instead idling a refinery; Chambishi Metals remained on care and maintenance for years afterwards.

name: Zero-rating of import duty on copper and cobalt concentrates (2020 budget)
description: Reversing the 2019 measure, the government cut import duty on copper and cobalt concentrates to 0% to restore feedstock economics for domestic smelters and refineries that toll-treat DRC material. The measure recognises that Zambian smelter capacity exceeds domestic concentrate supply, making imported feed integral to the value-addition chain.
entities: Ministry of Finance and National Planning
source_name: Mondaq - Zero Import Duty On Copper Concentrates (Zambia)
note: Snippet-based legal commentary.

name: 15% export duty on precious gemstones and metals
status: suspended (SI No. 4 of 2025, retroactive to 1 Jan 2025)
description: Introduced 1 January 2019 at 15% on gemstone and precious-metal exports, suspended from 1 January 2020 after industry pressure, abruptly reinstated 1 January 2025 (raising Kagem's effective revenue tax to 21% before 30% corporate tax), then re-suspended on 18 February 2025 by Statutory Instrument No. 4 of 2025 after Gemfields halted emerald sales. The whiplash illustrates the difficulty of taxing raw gemstone exports without in-country cutting capacity.
entities: Ministry of Finance and National Planning
source_name: National Jeweler - Zambia Reinstates 15% Export Duty on Precious Gemstones, Shocking Gemfields
note: Snippet-based; suspension confirmed by Lusaka Times (https://www.lusakatimes.com/2025/02/20/zambias-suspension-of-15-export-duty-on-precious-stones-economic-impact-and-expert-reactions/) and Gemfields Group statements.

name: Directive requiring emerald auctions to be held in Zambia (2013)
description: In April 2013 the Ministry of Mines, Energy and Water Development directed that all emerald auctions be held inside Zambia, arguing offshore sales (Gemfields auctioned in Singapore and Jaipur) caused capital flight and denied local dealers access. Gemfields was forced to move its June 2013 Singapore auction to Lusaka; the single-sales-point policy was later relaxed and Gemfields resumed international auctions alongside periodic Lusaka sales.
entities: Ministry of Mines, Energy and Water Development
source_name: Forbes - Zambia Ruling A Blow For Emerald Ambitions Of Gemfields
note: Snippet-based. Early example of marketing-stage (rather than processing-stage) value-capture policy.

name: Mines and Minerals Development Act No. 11 of 2015 (incl. 2022 royalty amendment)
description: The 2015 Act was Zambia's principal mining law, providing for mineral processing licences and local-preference obligations for goods, services and employment. The Mines and Minerals (Amendment) Act No. 29 of 2022 (effective 1 January 2023) restructured mineral royalty to a marginal-rate basis and restored its deductibility for income tax, improving economics for integrated mine-plus-processing operations.
entities: Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development
source_name: Afriwise - Understanding Zambia's Mining Law Overhaul
note: Snippet-based; amendment bill text at https://www.parliament.gov.zm/node/10738

name: Minerals Regulation Commission Act No. 14 of 2024
description: Establishes the Minerals Regulation Commission as an autonomous regulator (replacing direct ministry licensing), overhauls licence categories including mineral processing licences, and grants the state a minimum 30% golden-share/production-interest option in new mining licences. Together with the Geological and Minerals Development Act 2025 it replaced the 2015 Mines Act; it does not impose mandatory in-country processing but anchors the institutional machinery for value-addition regulation.
entities: Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development
source_name: National Assembly of Zambia - Minerals Regulation Commission Act, 2024 (Act No. 14)
note: Primary source (act text). Commentary: Afriwise and Bowmans (https://bowmanslaw.com/insights/zambia-mining-sector-undergoes-significant-overhaul-with-implementation-of-new-laws/).

name: Geological and Minerals Development Act No. 2 of 2025 - value addition provisions
description: Companion statute to the MRC Act; tasks government with developing incentives to attract mining investors and 'promote value addition and reinvestment', and obliges holders of mining rights and mineral processing licences to give preference to Zambian-made materials and citizen-owned contractors and suppliers. Provides the statutory hook for the 2025 local content regulations.
entities: Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development
source_name: ZambiaLII - Geological and Minerals Development Act, 2025
note: Primary source (consolidated act text on ZambiaLII).

name: Local content regulations - SI No. 68 of 2025 (preference for goods and services in mining)
description: The Geological and Minerals Development (Local Content) Regulations reserve a progressive share of core mining procurement for Zambian-owned or citizen-empowered companies - starting at 20% in 2026 and rising to at least 40% within five years - with a 15% price preference in bid evaluation. Non-core services (catering, security, haulage) are reserved exclusively for local companies, and miners must fund supplier development programmes at a minimum 0.05% of annual procurement spend.
entities: Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development
source_name: UNCTAD Investment Policy Monitor - Zambia introduces mandatory local content requirements
note: Snippet-based; legal analysis by Dentons (https://www.dentons.com/en/insights/articles/2025/october/23/the-geological-and-minerals-development-regulations).

name: National Critical Minerals Strategy (2024-2028)
description: Launched 29 August 2024, the strategy aims to stop raw export of critical minerals (cobalt, manganese, nickel, lithium, graphite, REEs) and promote domestic processing through policy reviews to limit raw-mineral exports, tax incentives for local processing industries, and a government fund for local value addition. It is paired with the 3-million-tonne copper target and flagship projects such as Africa's first cobalt sulphate refinery.
entities: Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development
source_name: DLA Piper Africa (Chibesakunda & Co) - Understanding Zambia's National Critical Minerals Strategy
note: Snippet-based legal analysis; launch reported by Copperbelt Katanga Mining (https://copperbeltkatangamining.com/zambia-to-launch-national-critical-minerals-strategy/).

name: MFEZ / priority-sector fiscal incentive regime (ZDA Act)
description: Under the ZDA Act, investors committing at least US$500,000 (foreign) or US$50,000 (local, threshold lowered to broaden access) in a Multi-Facility Economic Zone, industrial park or priority sector qualify for fiscal incentives including 0% corporate income tax for up to 10 years on zone profits and 0% import duty on machinery and capital goods for five years. The 2022 budget re-introduced enhanced MFEZ manufacturing incentives to drive value addition to raw materials.
entities: Ministry of Commerce, Trade and Industry
source_name: Zambia Development Agency - Investment Incentives
note: Primary source (ZDA); ZRA tax incentive schedule at https://www.zra.org.zm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/Tax-Incentives.pdf; 2022 re-introduction analysed by Bowmans (https://bowmanslaw.com/insights/corporate-services/zambia-re-introduces-fiscal-incentives-to-promote-manufacturing-in-economic-zones).

name: Chambishi MFEZ / Zambia-China Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone (ZCCZ)
description: Zambia's first declared MFEZ and China's first overseas economic and trade cooperation zone in Africa, developed by China Nonferrous Metal Mining Co (CNMC) at Chambishi on the Copperbelt. It anchors mineral value addition with the Chambishi copper smelter, acid plants, and dozens of processing and fabrication tenants; government ministers actively market it as the tax-free zone for adding value to copper.
source_name: World Bank - Multi-facility Economic Zones in Zambia (working paper)
note: Fetched via search; World Bank evaluation covers performance. Lusaka East MFEZ is a ZCCZ sub-zone opened 2009 focused on light industry and services.

name: Lusaka South Multi-Facility Economic Zone (LS-MFEZ)
description: Zambia's first state-owned economic zone, 15 km from central Lusaka, offering the standard MFEZ fiscal package plus dedicated power (600 MW ZESCO substation, 80 MW solar). By the mid-2020s it reported 164 approved investors and about US$1.68 billion in cumulative committed investment, including mineral-adjacent manufacturing, though it is less minerals-focused than Chambishi.
entities: Ministry of Finance and National Planning
source_name: Lusaka South MFEZ - official site
note: Primary source (zone operator); investment figure is operator-reported.

name: Zambia-DRC cooperation agreement on electric battery value chain
description: Signed 29 April 2022 in Lusaka with UNECA facilitation, committing the two countries (70%+ of world cobalt, ~10% of copper between them) to jointly develop battery precursor, battery and eventually EV manufacturing in transboundary special economic zones. A Council of Ministers and technical committees were set up, but by 2024-2026 the pre-feasibility study's status was unclear, plant siting was disputed, and no precursor plant had broken ground.
source_name: UNECA - Zambia and DRC Sign Cooperation Agreement to manufacture electric batteries
note: Primary source (UNECA). Status assessment: NRGI (https://resourcegovernance.org/publications/drc-zambia-battery-plant-key-considerations-governments-2024) reports conflicting statements on the feasibility study and disagreement over plant location.

name: Afreximbank-UNECA framework agreement and ARISE IIP pre-feasibility for BEV SEZs
description: In March 2023 Afreximbank and UNECA signed a framework agreement to establish special economic zones for battery-electric-vehicle production in DRC and Zambia, and engaged ARISE Integrated Industrial Platforms to run the pre-feasibility study (launched April 2023). ARISE presented findings to both governments in 2024; Zambian ministers said feasibility studies were 'done' in April 2024, but results were not published.
source_name: Afreximbank - Framework Agreement towards establishing Special Economic Zones for Battery Electric Vehicles in DRC and Zambia
note: Primary source (Afreximbank release); 'studies done' claim reported by News Diggers (https://diggers.news/business/2024/04/25/feasibility-studies-for-electric-vehicle-batteries-are-done-govt/).

name: US-DRC-Zambia MOU on electric vehicle battery value chains
description: Signed in December 2022 on the margins of the US-Africa Leaders Summit, the trilateral MOU commits the United States to support development of an integrated EV battery value chain from mine to precursor/cell assembly in DRC and Zambia, including feasibility support and investment facilitation. It is the US policy umbrella under which later Lobito Corridor and KoBold engagements in Zambia were framed.
source_name: SAFE (Securing America's Future Energy) - DRC-Zambia Issue Brief
note: Snippet/secondary source; original State Department media note of Dec 2022 referenced therein.

name: EU-Zambia Strategic Partnership on critical raw materials value chains
description: Non-binding MoU signed at the Global Gateway Forum in Brussels in October 2023, covering the entire raw-materials value chain with explicit emphasis on local value addition, ESG standards, infrastructure and skills. A joint operational roadmap of concrete actions was agreed within six months, under the EU Global Gateway programme (EUR 300 billion 2021-2027 envelope); EU-funded activities include gemstone skills training via the ILO.
source_name: European Commission - Global Gateway: EU signs strategic partnerships on critical raw materials value chains with DRC and Zambia
note: Primary source (EC press corner); roadmap detail at https://international-partnerships.ec.europa.eu/policies/global-gateway/critical-raw-materials-crm-partnership-roadmap-zambia_en

name: Lobito Trans-Africa Corridor and Zambia-Lobito rail (minerals corridor MOU)
description: A seven-party MOU (US, EU, Angola, DRC, Zambia, AfDB, Africa Finance Corporation) signed in October 2023 to develop the Lobito Corridor linking the Zambian-Congolese Copperbelt to the Atlantic; the greenfield Zambia-Lobito rail line has AFC as lead developer. US commitments reached roughly US$4 billion (total partner commitments ~US$6 billion) by December 2024, and KoBold Metals signed an MOU with AFC in October 2024 to anchor the Zambian leg with output from its Mingomba copper discovery - primarily an export-logistics play, but pitched as enabling processing investment along the corridor.
source_name: White House - FACT SHEET: Partnership for Global Infrastructure and Investment in the Lobito Trans-Africa Corridor
note: Primary source (archived White House fact sheet). value_usd is the cumulative US commitment to the corridor, not Zambia-specific.

name: 3 Million Tonnes Copper Production Strategy by 2031
description: The flagship national target to more than triple copper output to 3 million tonnes per year by 2031, built on brownfield revivals (KCM, Mopani ~1.4 Mt by 2030), greenfield projects and exploration, with an accompanying value-addition and local-content agenda; government cites ~US$14 billion in pledged and actualised mining investment. Production was 890,346 t in 2025 - the second straight year of growth but short of the interim 1 Mt target.
entities: Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development
source_name: Ministry of Mines and Mineral Development - Three Million Tonnes Copper Production Strategy by 2031
note: Primary source (ministry). Independent feasibility analysis: ZIPAR (https://zipar.org.zm/striking-while-the-irons-hot-zambias-strategy-to-triple-copper-output-by-2031/); 2025 output figure from African Leadership Magazine.

name: Kobaloni Energy cobalt sulphate refinery (Africa's first)
description: Kobaloni Energy, backed by Vision Blue Resources (Mick Davis) and the Africa Finance Corporation with roughly US$100 million, is building Africa's first cobalt sulphate refinery at Chambishi, one of few plants outside China able to make battery-grade cobalt sulphate. Government presented it as a flagship of the Critical Minerals Strategy with first output targeted for end-2025.
source_name: Mining.com / Bloomberg - Africa moves a step closer to continent's first cobalt refinery
note: Snippet-based; operational status as of 2026 not independently confirmed in sources reviewed.

name: Kasenseli Gold Mine (Zambia Gold Company)
description: State gold project in Mwinilunga, North-Western Province, developed by Zambia Gold Company with an initial ~K45 million injection for exploration and mining; conceived to feed a domestic gold refining and reserves-building chain rather than raw export. Mining was suspended by the Mines Safety Department in 2021-2022 (no gold sales in 2022) and President Hichilema officially re-opened the mine in November 2024.
entities: Ministry of Finance and National Planning
source_name: ZCCM-IH - Kasenseli Gold Mine Re-Opened
note: Primary source (ZCCM-IH announcements).

name: Gemstone Processing and Lapidary Training Centre (GPLTC), Ndola
description: Government training centre in Ndola offering a two-year gemstone cutting and polishing programme plus short courses in identification, grading and gemstone enterprise - the skills base for in-country emerald beneficiation. In 2025-2026 it received modern lapidary and gemmological equipment through an ILO/EU-supported project and a Kagem Mining donation (six cutting/polishing machines, sawing and calibrating machines) with a two-year partnership including student visits to the Lufwanyama emerald mine.
entities: Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development
source_name: Mining Weekly - Kagem donates gemstone processing equipment to Zambian training centre
note: Snippet-based; GPLTC official site: https://gpltc.ac.zm/. ILO/EU support reported July 2026.

name: EV battery manufacturing plant, Ndola (feasibility stage)
description: Government announced plans to start car/EV battery manufacturing 'before end of 2024', with a feasibility study for a plant in Ndola declared complete by Commerce Minister Chipoka Mulenga in April 2024, in partnership with Chinese investors and linked to the DRC-Zambia battery initiative. As of 2026 no plant had been commissioned and study results were not published.
entities: Ministry of Commerce, Trade and Industry
source_name: News Diggers - Feasibility studies for Electric Vehicle batteries are done - Govt
note: Snippet-based; 'before end of 2024' claim via Lusaka Provincial Administration (https://www.lsk.gov.zm/?p=2441).

name: Zambia Gold Company - national gold buying, processing and refining programme
description: ZGC (51% ZCCM-IH, 49% Ministry of Finance) has the mandate to mine, process, refine and market gold nationally: it buys gold from artisanal and small-scale miners, trains cooperatives in mechanised responsible mining, and plans a gold refinery producing bullion plus a jewellery beneficiation line. ZCCM-IH issued an EOI in October 2020 for a feasibility study into re-establishing a Precious Metals Plant (the old Ndola Copper Refinery PMP refined gold and PGMs 1977-2004).
entities: Ministry of Finance and National Planning
source_name: ZCCM-IH - ZCCM-IH and its investment strategy in the gold sector in Zambia
note: Primary source (ZCCM-IH); refinery EOI at https://www.zccm-ih.com.zm/2020/10/28/request-for-expressions-of-interest-eoi-for-a-consultant-to-conduct-a-feasibility-study-into-setting-up-a-precious-metals-plant/

name: Kabundi Resources manganese mining and washing (ZCCM-IH)
description: ZCCM-IH's wholly owned Kabundi Resources mines manganese at Kabundi, Serenje (Central Province), with mining from May 2020 targeting 20,000 t/month of ore; a first wash plant (~100 t/day) started September 2020 and a second 150 t/h plant was installed to lift washed-manganese output to ~10,000 t/month. ZCCM-IH also runs a Manganese Aggregation Pilot Project in Luapula Province to pool small-scale output, positioning for battery-grade manganese ambitions.
source_name: ZCCM-IH - Integrated Annual Report 2024
note: Primary source (annual report PDF, mirrored on minedocs); operational details also on ZCCM-IH investments pages.

name: IDC Zambia mining-sector beneficiation mandate
description: The Industrial Development Corporation, the state investment holding company (sole shareholder of ZCCM-IH's government stake and holder of 25% of Kagem Mining), promotes diversified exploration and mining of gold, gemstones, cobalt and manganese 'with emphasis on local beneficiation and value addition'. Its industrial portfolio includes mining-adjacent ventures and it has extended development financing to processing projects.
source_name: IDC Zambia - Mining sector page
note: Primary source (IDC).
